takeaways: A tour of a Lennar model in the Royal Oak community in Lake Elmo, on the east side of the Twin Cities: about 5,200 finished square feet (about 3,200 above grade), priced at just over $1 million when filmed.
Homes in the development were ranging from the high $900,000s to about $1.3 million, roughly $200 per square foot by Jason's math, with a community clubhouse and pool.

The layout includes a front sitting room and office, a formal dining room, a large kitchen island and walk-in pantry, an upstairs loft and laundry, and a very large owner's suite with a walk-in tile shower and separate water closet.
The finished walkout lower level adds a recreation area, another bedroom and bath, and generous storage. Every home in the neighborhood has a concrete driveway, which is unusual in Minnesota.

faq.q: What does $1 million buy in new construction in Lake Elmo?
faq.a: In this October 2025 tour, about 5,200 finished square feet with a finished walkout basement in Lennar's Royal Oak community, roughly $200 per square foot.

takeaways: The Twin Cities are adding about 17,000 new homes a year this decade, and some suburbs will look very different by 2050.

Lakeville built close to 4,900 homes from 2020 to 2025, the most in the metro, then voted 5-0 in April 2026 for a one-year pause on new plat approvals. More than a thousand approved lots and townhomes can still be built.
Woodbury built more than 4,200 homes over the same period, second-most in the metro; Washington County property taxes tend to run lower than Hennepin County's.
Maple Grove (about 3,600 new homes) and Blaine (about 2,700) are each forecast to add roughly 20,000 people by 2050: steady, proven demand.

Rosemount (about 3,200 new homes, growth of about 24% from 2020 to 2025) and Cottage Grove (about 2,300) are value plays with growth still ahead. Part of UMore Park in Rosemount is lined up for aerospace research.

Corcoran (about 36 square miles, much of it still farmland) is projected by the Metropolitan Council to grow from about 6,200 people in 2020 to nearly 19,600 by 2050. Carver, with its historic river downtown, is projected to nearly triple.
Jason's framework: Lakeville, Woodbury and Maple Grove are the safe bets; Rosemount and Cottage Grove the value plays; Corcoran and Carver the biggest change by percentage.

faq.q: Why did Lakeville pause new home building?
faq.a: After building close to 4,900 homes from 2020 to 2025, the city council voted 5-0 in April 2026 for a one-year pause on new plat approvals so the city could catch up. Already-approved lots can still be built.

faq.q: Which Twin Cities suburbs will grow the most by 2050?
faq.a: By percentage, places like Corcoran and Carver, which the Metropolitan Council projects to roughly triple. By number of homes, Lakeville, Woodbury, Maple Grove, Blaine and Rosemount keep adding the most.

takeaways: A 2022 tour of what $600,000 bought in new construction in Lakeville: a custom home by Peach Builders, a family-owned local builder.
About 2,200 finished square feet with four bedrooms upstairs, three baths, a main-floor office and a three-car garage with tall doors.
An open kitchen with quartz counters, a five-burner range and plenty of counter space; upstairs laundry; and an owner's bath with a walk-in tile shower and separate water closet.
The unfinished basement has 8-foot ceilings and is already plumbed for a bathroom, so it can be finished later without breaking concrete. The lot was sodded with irrigation.
Prices have changed since 2022; see the current Lakeville market report.

faq.q: What did $600,000 buy in Lakeville new construction in 2022?
faq.a: In this tour, about 2,200 finished square feet with four bedrooms, three baths and a three-car garage, plus an unfinished basement plumbed for another bathroom.

takeaways: "Investor-owned" means the owner has two or more homes they don't live in. That share of Twin Cities single-family homes has risen from about 1.5% in 2006 to about 3.5%, roughly 26,000 homes.

The largest owner, Tricon (part of Blackstone), holds more than 1,300 homes in the metro. Investors tend to favor suburban starter homes built after 1990 because parts are standard and repairs cheaper.
Big firms own only a small share; most investor buying is by local owners. The biggest effect is on suburban starter homes, where first-time buyers can get outbid.
If you get a cash offer letter, find out your home's true market value first. These offers usually come in below market, and listing as-is with a flexible closing date can often net more.
Buyers competing with investors: get a fully underwritten pre-approval, be ready to move within hours, offer flexible terms, and don't rule out homes that need some work.

faq.q: Should I accept a cash offer letter for my house?
faq.a: Not before you know your home's market value. Cash offers trade price for speed and convenience and usually come in below market; listing as-is on the open market can often put more in your pocket.

faq.q: How many Twin Cities homes do investors own?
faq.a: About 3.5% of single-family homes, roughly 26,000, are owned by investors with two or more homes they don't live in, up from about 1.5% in 2006, according to the video.

takeaways: Road work to plan around: Blaine's Highway 65 rebuild (2026 to 2029, heaviest in 2027, with stoplights replaced by overpasses), and phase two of I-494 (2027 to 2030) through Bloomington, Richfield, Edina and Eden Prairie.

Value picks, with prices as stated in the video: Shakopee (low $400,000s, now home to the new Mystic Lake Amphitheater), Cottage Grove (low $400,000s, among the fastest-growing) and Corcoran (high $500,000s to low $600,000s for larger lots).

Established suburbs: Eden Prairie (low $500,000s to low $600,000s, more than 1,000 acres of parks), Plymouth (high $400,000s to mid-$500,000s, about 1,800 acres of parks and three public beaches), Maple Grove (low to mid-$400,000s, Arbor Lakes) and Lakeville (high $400,000s to low $500,000s, paused new plat applications).
Lifestyle picks: Stillwater (river town on the St. Croix), Prior Lake (15 lakes in the city), White Bear Lake (walkable downtown, mid-$300,000s) and Carver (historic river downtown, low $500,000s).

Luxury: Edina (high $700,000s and up; Southdale was the first enclosed mall), Medina (horse properties and big lots, $1 million and up), and Orono and Wayzata on Lake Minnetonka, where lakefront runs into the millions.

faq.q: When will the Highway 65 construction in Blaine be finished?
faq.a: The rebuild started in June 2026 and is scheduled to wrap up in 2029, with the heaviest work and detours in 2027, according to the video.

faq.q: What are good value suburbs near Minneapolis?
faq.a: Jason points to Shakopee, Cottage Grove and Corcoran for value, with White Bear Lake among the easier places to get into at around the mid-$300,000s at the time of the video.

takeaways: Twin Cities home prices hit a record high for the 14th straight year, yet sales are slow, because roughly half of homeowners with a mortgage have a rate below 4%.
The math: a $400,000 loan at about 3% is roughly $1,700 a month in principal and interest; the same loan at about 6.5% is close to $2,500, almost $800 more.
Freddie Mac estimates a locked-in low rate is worth about $55,000 per household, and FHFA researchers found the lock-in effect prevented roughly 1.7 million home sales in two years.
With about two months of supply, buyers still compete for homes, even though new listings reached a three-year high.
Staying has costs too: owners now stay a record median of 11 years, and owning costs typically $16,000 to $21,000 a year nationally on top of the mortgage, whether the house fits or not.

Downsizing changes the math: a smaller loan can keep the payment close to what you pay now, and about one in three recent repeat buyers paid cash. Condos and townhomes offer more room to negotiate right now.
When rates ease, both buyers and sellers may come back at once, so being pre-approved and ready before then helps.

faq.q: Why is the Twin Cities housing market so slow?
faq.a: Roughly half of homeowners with a mortgage have a rate under 4%, so moving would raise their payment sharply. Fewer listings means buyers still compete, and prices keep setting records.

faq.q: Does downsizing make sense with higher rates?
faq.a: Often, yes. A less expensive home means a smaller loan, so the payment can stay close to what you pay now, and many downsizers use their equity to pay cash.
